newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson Multimedia to shut sites pre-sale.
newsitem.headline: Thomson Multimedia to shut sites pre-sale.

text.p: Thomson Multimedia (TMM), the consumer electronics unit of state-owned Thomson SA, will implement a fresh restructuring plan in 1997 in order to be privatised during 1998, industry sources said on Friday.

The restructuring had been demanded by the government after its decision on Wednesday to relaunch the privatisation of Thomson SA by the separate sale of 58-percent defence electronics unit Thomson-CSF and TMM, they said.
TMM would get a 10 billion franc ($1.9 billion) capital injection.
The Prime Minister's office and the Industry Ministry were not immediately available for comment.

The government suspended the privatisation sale of Thomson SA to Lagardere Groupe on December 4 because the independent Privatisation Commission could not agree with the terms of a planned re-sale of TMM to Daewoo Electronics of South Korea.
Daewoo chairman Soon-hoon Bae has said he is still a candidate to buy TMM.

The restructuring would lead to the closure of several of the group's 30 sites. According to the sources, between five and 10 of these sites concerned would be in the United States, Germany and southeast Asia. France, where 5,500 of TMM's 40,000 staff work, would not be touched.
TMM has three European brands -- Thomson, Telefunken and Saba -- as well as Ferguson in Britain and Brandt in France. In the U.S. market it uses the brands RCA, General Electric and Proscan.
Rival Philips Electronics has four European brands.
The restructuring aims at "significant" efficiency gains.
"Taking account of the pending capital increase, the 1997 net result should be better," said a company official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"A privatisation is possible during 1998 because the state could then put forward the excellent financial outlook related to the return of the General Electric licences which will be taken into account from 1999," he added.
When Thomson bought television activities in 1987 from General Electric Co, it obtained a lower price by granting GE the right to technology licence fees for 10 years.
TMM made a first-half 1996 loss of three billion francs after an operational loss of one billion francs, provisions of 1.2 billion francs and financial charges of 800 million francs.
Chairman Alan Prestat has indicated the operating result might be positive for the year but there would be a net loss.
"1996 is not a good year for any of the television producers. People prefer to buy computers instead," the official said, adding this could change in 1997.
The European Commission still has to approve the capital injection and is expected to attach a number of conditions to a go-ahead, probably a freeze on volumes.

"That will not really hurt us. TMM is at its optimum with a 21 percent market share in the U.S. and 22 percent in France. The closure of sites will not increase production volumes," the official said.

TMM will have debts of some 16 billion francs at the end of 1996, against 14 billion in 1995. The capital increase would allow a cut in financial costs of 500 to 600 million francs per year. With a rise in operating result this would allow a net profit in 1997.
The 1998 result would be even better and from 1999 the licence fees would add one billion francs per year to results, the official added. ($1=5.218 French Franc)
